ConsentRequest.description:
A grant or a withdrawal.

One purpose per request, because consent must be *specific* (Art. 4(11)). A
payload that accepted a list would let a client send one "I agree" covering
everything, which is exactly the shape the law rejects.

The outcome of redeeming a link.

Carries the user, so the profile screen can update without a second round

Everything the dashboard renders, in one request.

One round trip rather than four: the four headline tiles, the breakdown and

Separate from the overview by design — see `MetricsTrend`. The overview is

The whole wizard state, in one shape the client can render from cold.

`steps` and `missing` are sent rather than hard-coded in the client so that
adding a step is a backend change. A client with its own copy of the step
list is a client that disagrees with the server about where the user is.

Acknowledgement that a message is queued.

Not "sent". The outbox is drained by a worker, so the API cannot honestly
claim delivery at the moment it answers — and a client that shows "sent"
against a queue that later dead-letters has told the user something false.

VerifyEmailRequest.description:
Redeem a confirmation link.

A POST with the token in the body, not a GET with it in the path. Three
reasons, and the third is the one that decides it: a GET is retried by
proxies and prefetched by mail clients, tokens in a URL end up in server
logs and `Referer` headers, and a GET that changes state is wrong anyway.
The page reads the token out of the query string and posts it.

about the row is exposed — the id is internal and there is no endpoint that
takes it.

post.description:
Start a new token family.

A fresh family per login, rather than reusing one, is what makes "log out
everywhere" mean something later: revoking a family cannot take down a
session it never belonged to.

429.description: Ten attempts per fifteen minutes per origin. `extra.retry_after_seconds` says when to come back.

post.description:
Always succeeds.

No authentication is required and a missing cookie is not an error: logging
out twice, or logging out with an already-dead session, must both leave the
caller logged out. Returning 401 here would leave the cookie in the browser
on the one path where clearing it matters most.

get.description:
Resolve the bearer token to the account behind it.

The frontend calls this once on load, after refreshing, to decide whether to
render the app or the login page. It hits the database rather than trusting
the JWT's claims, which is what makes an erased account stop working before
its access token would have expired on its own.

401.description: Missing, malformed or expired access token.

post.description:
Spend the presented token and issue its successor.

The token arrives as a cookie and never as a body field: a body field would
mean JavaScript could read it, which is the exact property the httpOnly
cookie exists to deny (ADR-0003).

Replaying a spent token revokes the entire family — see
`RefreshTokenService.rotate`. That is the detection, and it is the reason
rotation is worth doing at all.

401.description: No cookie, an expired token, or — with code `auth.refresh_token_reused` — a replayed token, in which case the whole family has been revoked and the user must sign in again.

post.description:
Create the account and return a session in one round trip.

Registering then making the user log in is a second chance to lose them for
no security gain — the credentials were just verified by being chosen.

The confirmation email is *queued*, not sent, in this same transaction. Two
consequences worth being explicit about: a registration that rolls back
cannot leave a verification mail on its way to an account that does not
exist, and a mail provider being down cannot fail a signup. The account is
usable immediately; confirming the address is a separate, later act.

409.description: That email address is already registered.

429.description: Five registrations per hour per origin.

post.description:
Stamp the address as confirmed.

Unauthenticated on purpose. The link is followed from a mail client, which
may not be on the device that registered and will not carry the session
cookie — requiring auth here would mean the most common path (read mail on a
phone, registered on a laptop) is the one that fails. The token *is* the
credential, and it is single-use and short-lived precisely so it can be.

Note what this does not do: it does not sign the caller in. A link that
arrives by email and produces a session is a login bypass — anyone with read
access to the inbox, including a forwarding rule nobody remembers, would get
one.

422.description: The link is unknown, already used, or expired.

post.description:
Queue a fresh link for the caller's own address.

Authenticated, and takes no address. An endpoint that accepted one would
tell any account holder whether a *given* address is registered and
unconfirmed, and would let them point our sending reputation at it.

202, not 200: the message goes on the outbox and a worker sends it, so at
the moment this answers nothing has been delivered and claiming otherwise
would be a lie the client repeats to the user.

401.description: Missing, malformed or expired access token.

429.description: Three resends per hour per origin.

get.description:
Headline figures, the scrap breakdown and the tolerance bands.

Scoped to the signed-in user by `user.id`, never by a client-supplied line
id. An endpoint that takes the line from the query string is one missing
ownership check away from letting user A read user B's production data, and
that check is the kind that gets refactored out.

422.description: The account has no production line yet — code `metrics.no_line_configured`. Send the user back to onboarding.

charts and the cohort benchmark.

Returning 404 for "not started" would give the client two shapes to handle
for one situation. "Not started" is step `role` with no answers.

put.description:
Persist the position and the answers after every step.

This is what makes the wizard resumable across devices and across a browser
crash — the server, not the client, owns where the user is.

post.description: Turn the answers into a plant and a line, and close the wizard.

422.description: Required answers are still missing; `missing` names them.

get.description: Derived from the append-only log, never read from a boolean column.

post.description:
POST, never PUT or PATCH.

The verb is part of the design: this **appends an event**, it does not edit
a value. Withdrawal is the same endpoint with `granted: false`, because
Art. 7(3) requires withdrawing to be as easy as giving — and a separate
endpoint is where "as easy" quietly stops being true.

delete.description:
The brief's mandated offboarding, and Art. 17.

Not reversible, and deliberately not soft in effect even though it is soft
in mechanism: the row survives so the partial unique index can free the
email for re-registration, but every identifying column on it is scrubbed.
delete.summary: Erase this account and everything attached to it (Art. 17)

get.description:
`null` when none has ever been requested — not a 404.

"You have never asked for an export" is a normal state of the profile
screen, not an error, and modelling it as one would make the client handle a
failure path for the common case.

Deliberately unauthenticated — this is the landing page's only endpoint.

That also makes it the app's one anonymous write, which is why it is the
only route carrying a rate limit. The limiter counts against a salted hash
of the caller's IP; the address itself is never stored.

Liveness: the process is up.

Deliberately touches no dependencies — an orchestrator restarting the
container because Postgres blipped would make an outage worse, not better.

Readiness: this instance can serve traffic.

Currently trivial. Gains a database check and a job-queue check as those
